newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha tours protest-hit south.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha tours protest-hit south.

text.p: President Sali Berisha, touring Albania ahead of a presidential election, on Tuesday arrived in the ancient town of Berat where investors caught up in an investment scam burned government buildings last month.

Berisha, who must seek a fresh term as president in a vote in parliament by March 9, has travelled around the Balkan state in the past 10 days to gauge support after weeks of violent protests over the collapse of a string of high-yield, high-risk investment schemes.
Plain-clothes police were out in force in Berat, site of Albania's first settlement some 2,400 years ago, but there appeared to little enthusiasm among townsfolk to see Berisha.
Around 300 people in the southern hillside town of around 40,000 lined a street near a cinema where the president was due to deliver a speech to an invited audience.
Berisha has made few open-air appearances since the troubles erupted in January and most rallies are held indoors, packed with supporters of his right-wing Democratic Party.

Hundreds of thousands of people in Europe's poorest state of 3.4 million have lost their life savings in pyramid investment schemes which blossomed after the fall of the harsh Stalinist regime in 1990.
Riots broke out when investors learned they would receive little or no money back from five failed investment funds, whose collapse left thousands of families destitute.

Berisha has been at pains to assure savers that his government would do all it could to seize assets and pay them some of their money back. But he has also been blunt in insisting that the government, struggling with a huge budget deficit, would not use state funds or print money to reimburse investors.
He said Albanians had learned a hard lesson in the country's first embrace of capitalism.
While violent clashes have abated in the past two weeks, students nationwide have called for a boycott of lectures to force the dismissal of the Democratic Party government.
In Vlore, 100 km (60 miles) southwest of Berat, protestors have staged peaceful daily marches for three weeks.
A group of some 50 students there has gone on hunger strike over the financial scandal, but the action has drawn no reaction from Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government.
In Gjirokaster, near the Greek border, students boycotted classes for a second day and a growing number of faculties at Tirana University have also responded to the boycott appeal.
Protesters went on a rampage in Berat on January 26, burning the local law court, town hall and main police station.
Local sources say around 40 percent of Berat's population invested in the failed Gjallica pyramid scheme.

The town which once depended for its livelihood largely on the former Mao Zedong textile factory, which worked at full steam when communist Albania was a close friend of China up to 1978, but now operates at less than a quarter capacity.

Many townsfolk have been forced to depend on remittances by relatives working abroad. Greece and Italy now fear the crisis could spark a fresh wave of illegal emigration as the dream of impoverished Albanians to get rich quick is shattered.
